name: PT Bank of India Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank of India Indonesia: capital-rich, return-poor, priced for the float
frontmatter.summary: BSWD is a small, heavily capitalised Indonesian commercial bank whose shares are almost entirely held by its Indian parent and its affiliates. The business earns a return far below its cost of equity, needs no capital and cannot distribute cash until its deficit is cleared, so fundamental value sits far under the market price. We initiate at SELL with a Rp3,374 target: the float, not the franchise, sets the price, and the free-float step is a dated supply risk.
thesis: The franchise is real but idle: a capital adequacy ratio of 87.8% against a return on equity of 1.4% means most of the balance sheet earns a deposit-like yield and the equity base is roughly twice what the loan book can use [S12].

Earnings are small, thin and volatile: net profit fell from IDR78.8bn in FY2024A to IDR48.3bn in FY2025A on a provisioning charge that rose to IDR154.0bn, and the run-rate to August 2026 is IDR70.9bn [S12][S6].
Fundamental value is Rp14 a share against a price of Rp7,800: the market pays 8.0x book and 292.0x earnings for a bank that cannot distribute cash and does not need new capital [S12].

Ownership, not fundamentals, sets the marginal price: the controller and affiliates hold almost the whole register, the stock is on the exchange’s high-concentration list, and it has been suspended twice in the past year for disorderly trading [S2][S3][S4].

The free-float step due by 31 March 2027 cannot be met on-market in a stock that trades about Rp69,655,960 a day, and the company has not chosen a route: the instrument it has twice used - a preemptive rights issue - is carried as a bear-case dilution, not booked into a base case that cannot hold the proceeds. We initiate SELL with a Rp3,374 target and a -56.7% return [S6][S12].

catalysts.event: First staged free-float step for issuers above the exchange's capitalisation threshold, and the deadline the company has set for its study of how to meet the requirement
Final free-float step for issuers above the capitalisation threshold
Full-year 2026 audited accounts - the first test of the deposit run-off and the credit-cost run-rate

Exchange trading curbs, suspension or re-admission on disorderly price moves in a thin float

blocks.text: **SELL. Twelve-month target Rp3,374, a return of -56.7% from Rp7,800.**

PT Bank of India Indonesia Tbk is a commercial bank with a loan book of IDR4,189.1bn, deposits of IDR3,617.7bn and equity of IDR3,512.3bn at the end of FY2025A, and a market capitalisation of IDR28,773.2bn at the last close [S12]. The two numbers sit in different worlds. The bank earns a return on equity of 1.4% on audited FY2025A figures, carries a capital adequacy ratio of 87.8%, has never paid a dividend and holds an accumulated deficit of IDR253.7bn in unappropriated retained earnings [S12]. The price pays 8.0x book value and 292.0x our FY2026E earnings for that.

Our view is not that the bank is worthless. It is that the listed share is a float instrument first and a claim on a bank second. Bank of India holds 91.0% of the register and the exchange's concentration study attributes 100.0% to the controller and its affiliates, against a public free float of 7.7% on the exchange's own measure [S2]. The stock is on the high shareholding concentration list and has moved in violent steps around suspension and re-admission [S2][S3][S4]. On our numbers the fundamental twelve-month value is Rp14 a share. The engine concentrated-ownership lens, which is a regime variable rather than a valuation input, assumes the market gives back only part of an extreme premium over the next year and arrives at Rp3,374 - still a -56.7% return.

Three things move the value. First, the margin: net interest income of IDR166.9bn in the eight months to August 2026 annualises well below the FY2025A figure, and the deposit base that funds it fell to IDR3,300.0bn [S6]. Second, credit: a provisioning charge of IDR154.0bn in FY2025A - of which IDR36.4bn was foreclosed-collateral provisioning rather than lending loss - against an allowance balance of only IDR63.7bn and gross non-performing loans of 5.6% means coverage is thin and the charge stays high [S12]. Third, the regime: under the exchange's staged free-float rule the public holding of 7.7% must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and 15.0% by 31 March 2028, the company has not chosen how, and the stock trades too little to close the gap on-screen [S25][S6].

Indonesian commercial banks are grouped by core capital into tiers, and the smallest tier contains a long tail of institutions that are sub-scale relative to the large private and state banks. Sub-scale banks in that tier generally earn narrower margins, carry weaker fee franchises and depend on price-sensitive time deposits for funding, which makes their profitability sensitive to the policy rate cycle and to deposit competition from digital banks. The supervisor has been encouraging consolidation in that tier, and the exchange has tightened free-float and concentration rules that treat thinly traded, closely held stocks differently from widely held ones. None of this is specific to this company and none of it is sourced evidence for the numbers above.

BSWD is a single-segment Indonesian commercial bank. It takes deposits from the public and lends to small and mid-sized businesses and to individuals, and it invests the remainder of its balance sheet in placements with Bank Indonesia, in other banks and in securities [S12]. The annual report splits the loan book into working-capital, investment, export-import and consumption facilities, with the corporate and commercial pieces carrying the bulk of the book [S12]. On the funding side it runs current accounts, savings accounts and time deposits, and the mix is the story: low-cost funds were 19.0% of deposits at the end of FY2025A, so roughly four-fifths of the funding base is price-sensitive time money [S12].

The institution is old and small. It began as a people’s credit bank in Surabaya, became a commercial bank under the Bank Swadesi name, moved its head office to Jakarta, and took the Bank of India Indonesia name in 2011 after the Indian parent acquired control; the network was built out through branches in Surabaya, Jakarta, Bandung and Makassar and has since been trimmed, with sub-branches opened and cash offices closed [S12]. It employed 215 people at the end of FY2025A across the head office and the branch network [S12]. By any measure it is a challenger with no national distribution: the branch footprint is concentrated in a handful of cities and the bank competes for the same corporate and commercial borrowers as institutions many times its size [S12].

The capital history is the structure, not a footnote. The bank has twice gone to shareholders for new money through preemptive rights issues: PUT IV in 2022 issued 1,389m new shares at Rp1,000 each, and PUT V in 2023 issued 1,300m more, taking the count to 3,689m shares [S12 pp.18, 34]. Both were made to meet the minimum core-capital requirement, and both were needed because the accumulated deficit in unappropriated retained earnings stands at IDR253.7bn after years of thin profit [S12]. That is the record against which the free-float step should be read: the demonstrated instrument is a rights issue, and the bank has no history of a controlling shareholder placing down its stake.

The group structure is the defining feature. Bank of India, the Indian state-owned bank, is the controlling shareholder with 91.0% of the shares; the exchange's concentration study, counting identified holdings in scrip and book-entry form, attributes 100.0% to the controller and its affiliates when it designated the stock as high-concentration [S2]. Those figures are not complements of the exchange-measured public free float of 7.7%: the concentration measure counts identified holdings, including book-entry and nominee positions, while the float measure counts the public tranche, so we do not present one as the remainder of the other and say here which measure drives what. Under the exchange's staged rule for issuers above the capitalisation threshold, the public holding must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and 15.0% by 31 March 2028; at 7.7% the first step is 4.8% of the shares and the final step is larger [S25]. The company says it is studying options with an external and independent party and has not decided a corporate action [S6]. The subsidiary role inside the group is narrow: the Indonesian entity gives the parent a licensed presence and a corporate-banking bridge for Indian trade flows, but the annual report shows no material intra-group funding or asset flows, and related-party time deposits were 0.01% of the total time deposit book [S12].

Strategy as the board states it is defensive and regulatory. The annual report’s own direction to management is to meet the regulatory ratios in the work plan, follow up internal-control findings from OJK, internal audit and the external auditor, grow low-cost funds, and develop mobile banking and other products [S12]. The business plan embedded in the report targets a loan book of IDR4,189.1bn rising towards the levels management set for the plan years, with deposit growth meant to fund it [S12]. We take the plan as evidence of intent rather than as a forecast: eight months into FY2026 the loan book had grown to IDR4,760.0bn while deposits had fallen to IDR3,300.0bn, which is the opposite of the plan’s funding assumption [S6].

The Indonesian banking industry is large, profitable in the aggregate and brutally tiered. The largest banks earn returns on equity in the high teens on cheap current-account funding and national distribution; the smallest licensed banks earn a fraction of that, compete for price-sensitive deposits and carry cost bases that do not scale [S13]. BSWD sits in the smallest capital tier, which the supervisor has publicly identified as the segment where consolidation is being discussed, with OJK saying that several banks in that tier plan to consolidate and that the decision rests with each bank’s shareholders on business and corporate-strategy grounds [S13]. That is the single most important industry fact for this name: the regulator wants fewer, larger banks at the bottom of the market, and the parent’s stake is the asset that a transaction would reprice [S13].

Competitive position is weak on every axis we can source. Distribution is a handful of branches against national networks [S12]. Funding is dominated by time deposits at an average rupiah rate of 4.6% in FY2025A, slightly below the 4.6% paid a year earlier [S12]. That is the flow measure - the average rate actually paid - and it is the one we use throughout; the year-end stock rate in the interest-rate note is a different number on a different date and we do not mix the two. On the flow measure the cost of time money fell, not rose, and only marginally: the observed move is consistent with a back book that reprices slowly, not with a bank that passes a policy move through to depositors, and because the house macro deck carries no citable policy-rate average for the two years being compared we do not attach a historical deposit beta number to it. The practical read is that the cost of deposits is sticky in both directions, which limits how far the margin can fall but also leaves no funding-cost windfall to bank; we hold the forecast time-deposit cost near its FY2025A level against a flat policy path [S12]. The loan-to-deposit ratio of 115.8% at the end of FY2025A means the bank already lends more than it gathers and must top up with wholesale or interbank funding, which caps how fast it can grow without repricing deposits [S12]. Asset quality is below the industry’s comfort zone, with gross non-performing loans of 5.6% in FY2025A after 6.0% in FY2024A and a public-expose reading of 6.1% at November 2025, so the bank is not outgrowing its problem loans, it is managing them [S12][S8].

Porter’s five forces, applied honestly, all point the same way for a bank this size. Buyer power is high because depositors can move to a digital bank in minutes and borrowers can price-shop every renewal. Supplier power is high because funding is time-deposit-dominated and the marginal rupiah is auctioned. New entrants are numerous in the form of digital banks and fintech lenders, even if licensing is closed. Substitutes are strong in payments and in capital-markets products for the corporate clients the bank wants. Rivalry is intense in the small-commercial segment where every mid-sized bank competes. The only structural offset is capital: a capital adequacy ratio of 87.8% means the bank cannot be forced to shrink by a capital shortfall, and it can absorb losses that would close a competitor [S12].

The moat assessment is therefore nil on the business and strong on the licence. There is no cost advantage, no switching cost of consequence and no network effect in a bank with this footprint; what protects the franchise is the banking licence, the capital base and the parent’s willingness to keep it capitalised [S12]. That is why the value of the equity here is better read as the value of a licensed, over-capitalised shell inside a group that may or may not transact it, rather than as the present value of a lending franchise.

The regulatory frame has also become a price driver rather than a footnote. The exchange now enforces a minimum public free float that steps up for closely held names, publishes a high-shareholding-concentration list that removes affected stocks from the main indices, and suspends stocks whose prices move in a disorderly way [S2][S3][S6]. For a bank with a public holding of 7.7%, these rules are not background - they are the mechanism that decides who can own the stock and at what price [S2][S6].

Indonesian banking regulation is built around capital tiers, minimum capital, lending and liquidity ratios, and a supervisory expectation that small banks consolidate rather than remain sub-scale indefinitely. Free-float and shareholding-concentration rules exist because thinly traded, closely held stocks can be moved by small flows and are poor candidates for index inclusion. Rates, liquidity conditions and deposit competition from digital banks affect every bank in the market, but the magnitude differs sharply between the large banks with current-account franchises and the small banks that fund themselves with time deposits. This paragraph is context only and carries no source for the company-specific figures above.

**The history is flat, then volatile.** Across FY2023A to FY2025A the loan book moved from IDR3,716.2bn to IDR4,189.1bn, deposits from IDR2,700.8bn to IDR3,617.7bn, net interest income from IDR254.6bn to IDR289.4bn and other operating income from IDR12.6bn to IDR42.7bn [S12]. Net profit moved the other way in FY2025A, falling to IDR48.3bn from IDR78.8bn because the combined provision charge rose to IDR154.0bn from IDR102.9bn while other operating expenses rose to IDR114.7bn from IDR108.0bn [S12]. The revenue line was almost unchanged; the cost and credit lines were not. That is the shape of this bank’s earnings: a stable spread business squeezed by a provisioning cycle it cannot outgrow.

**Reconciliation to the audited accounts, and where the model reads from.** The other-operating-income note [S12 p.174] splits FY2025A other operating income into recovery of written-off loans IDR37.8bn, fees and commissions IDR3.0bn, net FX gain IDR1.3bn and other IDR0.6bn, which sum to the IDR42.7bn total [S12]. The provisioning note [S12 p.245] splits the IDR154.0bn charge into loans IDR117.6bn, placements and foreclosed collateral (AYDA) IDR36.4bn [S12 p.245]. The bank template's history lines for net interest income and non-interest income, however, read the data pack's narrower presentation: the pack shows IDR281.3bn of net interest income and IDR19.8bn of non-interest income against the audited IDR289.4bn and IDR42.7bn [S12]. The IDR31.4bn other-items line in the FY2025A column of the table above is exactly that presentation gap - it is what makes the model's reported profit before tax tie to the audited statement - and it is not carried forward: from FY2026E the line is the audited non-operating item of IDR0.4bn [S12]. The two forecast income lines do not sit on the same base and we say which is which: net interest income is built on the audited basis, reproducing the eight-month actual of IDR166.9bn annualised on the funded balance sheet, while non-interest income is grown 5.0% from the data pack's narrower line of IDR19.8bn, not from the audited IDR42.7bn, because the audited figure is dominated by the IDR37.8bn recovery of written-off loans and we do not capitalise that spike [S6][S12]. Nothing is double-counted: the pack's non-interest base already excludes the audited recovery, and the other-items line above is the only place the presentation gap is recognised. We flag the template limitation rather than model around it.

**Revenue build.** Our forecast starts from the audited FY2025A base and the FY2026 run-rate. Loans grow 14.0% in FY2026E, following the actual increase to IDR4,760.0bn at August 2026 from IDR4,189.1bn at December 2025, and then slow to 8.0% a year because deposits fell to IDR3,300.0bn over the same eight months and the loan-to-deposit ratio is already above the level the bank can sustain [S6][S12]. Deposits shrink -6.0% in FY2026E and then rebuild at 12.0% as the bank competes for time money; the fall reported in October is the June-to-August move, while the eight-month year-to-date decline is smaller, and we use the year-to-date level, not the quoted rate, as the base [S6][S12]. The margin input is 3.5% on the funded balance-sheet base, recovering to 4.1% by FY2030E; FY2026E reproduces the actual eight-month net interest income of IDR166.9bn annualised on the assets that actually stand behind it, not the audited FY2025A ratio of 4.3%, because the run-rate is what the bank is actually earning [S6][S12]. The deposit side is the reason the recovery stops where it does. On the flow measure the bank paid an average of 4.57% for rupiah time deposits in FY2025A against 4.64% in FY2024A, a marginal decline: the observed move is small and it is down, so it does not evidence a bank passing policy moves through, and the house macro deck has no citable policy-rate average for those two years on which to fit a historical beta. We therefore state the measure and the direction rather than a beta number, hold the forecast time-deposit cost near its FY2025A level against the house BI path of 5.8%, and keep the CASA share flat at 19.0% of deposits. The margin returns to the last audited effective ratio and not above it: a bank whose funding cost is sticky in both directions has no windfall to bank when the rate path flattens.

**Costs and credit.** The model runs one cost path, and it is the one stated here: opex is held at the audited FY2025A IDR114.7bn in FY2026E - IDR114.7bn in the model, the same figure to the rupiah - and then grows every year at a constant nominal rate, taking it to IDR120.5bn in FY2027E and IDR139.5bn in FY2030E [S12]. That rate is the one the cti inputs encode, not an independent ratio forecast: each year's cti is the stated rupiah cost divided by the modelled total operating income, which is why the cost-to-income ratio rises to 43.0% in FY2027E while income is still near the eight-month run-rate and the cost base grows faster than it, before falling to 36.7% by FY2030E as income growth catches up [S12]. The rate is below the increase the bank actually delivered in FY2025A (opex of IDR114.7bn against IDR108.0bn), so it is a real-terms cost increase, not a cost programme and not a cut [S12]. The FY2025A comparison point is the audited ratio - opex IDR114.7bn against total income of net interest IDR289.4bn plus other operating income IDR42.7bn - not the higher ratio the table above prints on the data pack's narrower income lines. Credit cost is the swing factor: 0.6% in FY2026E, low because the first eight months ran without the asset-quality top-ups that hit FY2025A, then normalising to 3.1% [S6][S12]. On the loan book, that terminal rate is deliberately above the FY2024A and FY2025A loan-only provisioning rates and above their three-year average - the IDR154.0bn combined charge overstated the lending loss because IDR36.4bn of it was foreclosed collateral - because the through-cycle charge, not a fitted average, is what the allowance position requires [S12]. It is also what coverage needs: the allowance of IDR63.7bn covers barely a quarter of the impaired stock implied by gross non-performing loans of 5.6%, and lifting that cover to half takes a one-off provision of about one and a quarter per cent of loans, which is exactly the step we put into the bear case rather than leaving out of the base [S12].

**Balance sheet, capital and liquidity.** Equity was IDR3,512.3bn at the end of FY2025A and we carry it to IDR3,753.1bn by FY2030E with no dividend until the deficit is cleared and no share issue in the base case, because no corporate action has been decided [S12][S6]. The capital ratio stays enormous throughout, well above any regulatory requirement, because retained earnings add to a base the loan book cannot absorb [S12]. The liquidity side is the constraint: deposits of IDR3,617.7bn fund loans of IDR4,189.1bn, an LDR of 115.8%, and the funding mix is four-fifths time deposits [S12]. Net interest income is charged on the funded balance sheet, not on a multiple of loans: the earning-asset base of IDR7,050.7bn in FY2026E is the deposits of IDR3,400.7bn plus the equity of IDR3,610.8bn plus the other liabilities the FY2025A balance sheet carries, an identity that holds to within a rounding line (the residual is the rounded other-liabilities amount), or 1.48 times loans, falling to 1.35 by FY2030E as the loan book outgrows the deposit base and the securities and placement book is run down to fund it [S12]. That is the correction made in this revision: the first draft held the multiple flat at the FY2025A level, which charged a margin on assets no deposit or capital stood behind. Net interest income is IDR250.4bn in FY2026E on that base and return on equity is 2.8%, and the accumulated deficit is not cleared until FY2031, so the first dividend is declared on FY2031 profit - both timings follow from the funded base and the corrected cost path, not from a policy choice [S12]. The bank template also carries a total-assets line that grosses loans up at the FY2025A asset-to-loan ratio; it is not published in the summary table and it does not feed net interest income, which is why the funded identity above, not that line, is the balance sheet this valuation uses.

**Earnings quality.** The accruals screen that applies to industrials is not meaningful for a bank, so we run the provisioning test instead. Provisions rose to IDR154.0bn in FY2025A from IDR102.9bn in FY2024A while gross non-performing loans fell to 5.6% from 6.0%, which is the right direction but on a thin buffer: the allowance balance of IDR63.7bn covers well under half of the impaired stock implied by those two figures [S12]. We read that as an optics-class flag, not a manipulation-class one - the charge is disclosed, the policy is standard and the auditor signed an unqualified opinion dated 27 March 2026 - but it means earnings are not yet clean and the through-cycle charge stays above the current run-rate [S12]. Two further items flatter book value and profit: a revaluation surplus of IDR115.1bn inside equity, so part of book value is an appraisal rather than accumulated earnings, and a recovery of written-off loans of IDR37.8bn booked in other operating income, which is the single largest line in that income [S12]. The other-items line in the FY2025A column of the table is the data-pack presentation gap explained above, not an operating item, and it disappears from the forecast [S12].

**The company's own plan, and why we sit below it.** The business plan in the annual report projects a return on equity of 3.7% in 2026, 3.8% in 2027 and 4.6% in 2028, on a net interest margin of 4.2% in 2026 [S12 p.47]. Our path is 2.8% in FY2026E, 1.3% in FY2027E and 0.8% in FY2028E, on a margin of 3.5% in FY2026E. The discount is evidenced rather than assumed: in FY2025 the bank delivered 43.1% of its net-profit target and 93.4% of its net-interest-income target [S12 p.13], so the plan's profit line is the part that has historically failed while its income line broadly held. The plan's ROE also needs the margin to recover to its stated path and the credit charge to stay near zero; we take the plan's loan and deposit ambitions as evidence of intent where the eight-month run-rate supports them, use the actual margin, and carry a positive through-cycle credit cost. That is the whole of the downward drift from the plan, and it is sourced to the delivery record, not to caution [S12][S6].

**What we forecast.** Net profit to parent is IDR98.5bn in FY2026E, IDR46.2bn in FY2027E and IDR35.4bn in FY2030E, with EPS of Rp27 falling to Rp10 - FY2026E is the peak because it carries the low credit cost, and the cost line then grows while the margin only partly recovers [S12][S6]. FY2026E sits below the annualised eight-month run-rate, and deliberately: the run-rate takes the IDR70.9bn earned in eight months and repeats it for four more with no second-half credit charge, while we hold opex at last year's rupiah amount and carry a positive credit cost, which is what closes the gap between the two. Return on equity stays in the low single digits throughout at 2.8% and 0.9%, which is the number that matters for valuation: no plausible operating path takes this bank to a return above its cost of equity within the forecast horizon [S12].

**Data gaps we are working around.** There is no third-quarter FY2026 statutory report on file; the latest operating data are the eight-month figures published in October 2026, and we have not reconciled the August deposit figure to the September balance sheet [S6]. The data pack carries a cash-flow statement that is meaningless for a bank and we do not use it. The audited FY2025A net interest income of IDR289.4bn and other operating income of IDR42.7bn are not marginal to the pack's IDR281.3bn and IDR19.8bn: the gaps are large, they are disclosed in the reconciliation above, and the bank template will only take the pack's lines for those two history fields, so the audited figures are carried as facts and quoted here rather than restated in the table [S12]. The forecast is on the audited basis for net interest income, which is the line that carries the value, and on the data pack's narrower base for non-interest income as stated above; the difference between the two bases is disclosed rather than netted.

We value BSWD as a bank, which means equity-side methods on book value and return, not enterprise free cash flow [S12]. The method set is the house bank card: justified price-to-book as the primary at 50%, residual income at 30% and dividend discount at 20% [S12].

The cost of equity is 12.5%: the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, the sovereign default spread of 1.6% deducted, an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, and an unlevered beta of 1.00 with no debt in the capital structure [S12]. Because the bank carries no financial debt the weighted cost equals the cost of equity [S12].

Three parts of that build need arguing, and we argue them against the VAL_BANKS tests rather than assert a plain build. First, the band test is the total premium over the risk-free rate: the yield less the default spread plus beta times the mature premium plus the country premium nets to a premium of more than five points, inside the house IDR band; the individual 4.2% mature premium is not the band test, and reading it alone would double-count the country premium that sits next to it. Second, beta: the house default is a large-bank median, and this is the smallest name in the sector with gross NPL of 5.6%, allowance coverage near a quarter and a public float of 7.7%, so we override the default and the beta is a company parameter in the model, not the industry default [S12]. Third, we do not stack the risks twice: the non-performing loans, the thin float and the trading suspensions are already in the beta and in the 30% liquidity discount applied below, and charging them again in the COE would be a cautious base case, which the house card forbids. The result sits at the level of the large-bank peer build rather than below it, and this is the smallest name carrying it; the sensitivity of the target to the cost of equity is in the table above, and a full percentage point in either direction does not change the rating.

The primary method produces Rp12 a share. Justified price-to-book is 0.01 on a sustainable return on equity of 0.4% against a cost of equity of 12.5% and terminal growth of 0.3% [S12]. Both of those last two inputs are tested against each other: the growth rate must sit at or below ROE times one minus payout, and at the modelled terminal ROE and a payout of 30.0% the cap is a little above the 0.3% we use, so the perpetual growth this bank can fund is close to zero [S12]. A bank that earns a small fraction of its cost of equity and cannot grow book without adding capital it does not need is worth a tiny fraction of its book value, and the arithmetic says so [S12]. Book value per share was Rp952 at the end of FY2025A and we carry Rp1,017 by FY2030E because earnings are retained [S12].

The cross-checks differ in degree and we say why. Residual income gives Rp0 a share, at its zero floor: from the same book value it charges the cost of equity against the full equity base and fades growth to the terminal rate, and because the forecast return on equity never exceeds the cost of equity the present value of the residual stream is negative, so the leg floors at zero rather than printing a negative value [S12]. The dividend discount model gives Rp8, below the primary, and the divergence is disclosed rather than smoothed: the first distribution is legally available only once the accumulated deficit of IDR253.7bn is cleared, which our forecast does during FY2031, so the method discounts a stream that starts on FY2031 profit at a payout of 30.0% and capitalises it at terminal growth of 0.3% [S12]. A third of a small and shrinking profit, grown at almost nothing, is worth less than the book the primary method marks to the same return - which is the honest arithmetic for an over-capitalised bank, and the reason the two legs diverge by more than the house tolerance. We keep the dividend method at its house weight rather than lift it on a policy assumption, and we do not drop it either: the payout is our choice, the controller's record is retention, and dropping the method would flatter the valuation [S12].

There is no valuation bridge, and that is deliberate. For a bank the equity-side methods already value the whole balance sheet through book value and return, so an enterprise-value bridge would double-count the deposits and the loan book; nothing after the 31 December 2025 balance-sheet date is a completed transaction, a declared dividend, an asset sale or a capital raise that belongs in one. The material post-balance-sheet events - the HSC designation, the free-float study, the eight-month operating results and the two suspensions - are in the text and in the forecast calibration, not in a bridge [S2][S3][S6][S12].

The probability-weighted scenario value is Rp21 a share before the liquidity adjustment; the base-case method blend is Rp8, and the business scenarios that surround it are in the risk section. We apply a 30% discount because average daily traded value is about Rp69,655,960 and the public float is 7.7%, and the data pack records a meaningful number of zero-volume days over the past three months [S12]. That discount is a statement about how little stock trades, not about the bank. After it, the twelve-month fundamental value is Rp14 a share, and the standing value is Rp8 [S12].

**The asset floor, and why it does not save the price.** A bank like this has to be tested on what the equity would be worth run off or sold, not only on its earnings. The answer is close to book: equity of IDR3,512.3bn sits on a balance sheet that is mostly cash, Bank Indonesia placements and securities, so book value per share of Rp952 is the realistic ceiling for a break-up, a capital release or a licence sale to an OJK-sponsored consolidator under the KBMI I consolidation push [S12][S13]. That ceiling does not support the market price: the price stands at 8.0x times our FY2026E book value of Rp979 and 8.2x times the FY2025A reported book of Rp952 quoted here, and no credible transaction pays a multiple of book anywhere near that for a bank earning a small fraction of its cost of equity. We do not put the floor into the fundamental value, because it is a control value available only through a transaction that would trigger a tender offer and none is sourced; we keep the going-concern value as the anchor and show the floor so a reader can hold both. It is also the largest single risk to our SELL, and it runs the wrong way for the price: a buyer at around book would be a negative catalyst from here, not a rescue.

**The konglo lens.** BSWD is a concentrated-ownership name, so the fundamental value above is the anchor and the lens is applied separately. Price divided by the spot fundamental value - the twelve-month value of Rp14 discounted back one year at the cost of equity, or Rp13 - is 605.5 times, and that is the number a reader can reproduce from Rp7,800 [S12]. The market is paying a premium of that order, which is also what 8.0x book and 292.0x our FY2026E earnings say [S12]. The lens does not assume the gap closes in full over the next year. The house regime framework assumes the closing share of the log premium rises with the name’s flags, and here the base regime closes about 0.40 of it, giving a regime target of Rp677 [S12]. The bear regime, which assumes faster compression, gives Rp52; the bull regime, which assumes the flow premium persists, gives Rp12,090 [S12]. Probability-weighted, the lens target is Rp3,374 [S12].

We think that is the most likely path for this name, and we want to be explicit about why. The premium is not a forecast about earnings; it is the price of a scarce float in a stock where the controller holds 91.0% and the public holds 7.7% [S2]. Three regime facts decide whether it persists. The stock is on the exchange’s high-concentration list, which removes it from the main indices and narrows the buyer pool [S2]. The free-float deadline of 31 March 2027 requires the public holding to step up from 7.7% towards 12.5%, with the 15.0% final a year later, a first-step gap of 4.8% of the shares over the next 4.7 months, and management has said it is studying options with an independent adviser without choosing one [S25][S6]. And the stock has already been suspended twice for disorderly trading in the past year, with the price moving in cumulative jumps the exchange called unreasonable [S3][S4]. In that setting, keeping part of an extreme premium for another year is more likely than either full convergence or indefinite persistence - which is precisely what the lens assumes, and precisely why the target still sits -56.7% below the price.

**What the price implies.** At Rp7,800 the market values the equity at 8.0x our FY2026E book and 292.0x our FY2026E earnings, on a dividend yield of zero [S12]. Read backwards, the price is not a statement about the lending business at all: it is a call option on a change of control, a strategic transaction or a liquidity event, priced by a few percent of the shares changing hands. We do not underwrite that option, because we have no sourced evidence of a transaction, and we would rather state the fundamental value plainly and let the lens carry the part of the premium the regime says is most likely to persist [S12][S13].

Banks are valued on equity-side methods because the balance sheet is the business: deposits are raw material, loans are the product, and book value is a meaningful anchor in a way it is not for an industrial company. Justified price-to-book ties the multiple to the spread between sustainable return on equity and cost of equity, and residual income arrives at the same place by discounting the value created above the cost of capital. Thinly traded stocks with small public floats trade away from those anchors for long periods because the marginal seller is scarce and the marginal buyer is flow-driven; that gap is a market-structure phenomenon rather than an earnings forecast. This paragraph is method context and carries no company figures.

**Downside risks, ranked by likelihood times impact.** Governance and ownership concentration is the highest: the controller holds 91.0%, the public owns 7.7%, the exchange counts 100.0% in identified hands, and the stock carries a formal high-concentration designation, which means index exclusion and a narrower buyer base regardless of what the bank earns [S2]. Likelihood high, impact high. Liquidity is next: average daily traded value of about Rp69,655,960 and repeated zero-volume days mean an exit is a price event, not a process, and the stock has been suspended for exactly this kind of disorderly move [S3][S4]. Likelihood high, impact high for anyone who needs to sell. Regulatory free-float compliance is the third, and it is a supply event rather than a mechanical one: the public holding must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and 15.0% by 31 March 2028, a first-step gap of 4.8% of the shares that is worth far more than a year of the stock's traded value at the current price, so it cannot be absorbed on-screen [S25]. The company has not chosen the route. We do not book a rights issue in the base case: the bank template cannot carry paid-in capital, so booking the dilution without the proceeds would be a one-way haircut to book value and the dividend stream, and no action has been decided in any case [S6][S12]. The dilution is carried as a bear-case shock instead - on top of the credit and margin shocks, not instead of them - and if an issue is announced and priced the base case will carry it together with its cash. Likelihood high, impact medium to high, and the dilution is modelled in the bear case rather than assumed away.

Credit risk sits in the middle. Gross non-performing loans were 5.6% in FY2025A and the allowance balance of IDR63.7bn is thin against that stock, so a second provisioning cycle would hit a profit line of IDR98.5bn hard [S12]. Likelihood medium, impact high on earnings and low on solvency, because the capital ratio of 87.8% absorbs almost anything [S12]. Margin and funding risk follows: deposits fell to IDR3,300.0bn by August 2026, the loan-to-deposit ratio is 115.8% and four-fifths of funding is time money at an average rate of 4.6%, so the bank is a price-taker in its own funding market [S6][S12]. Likelihood medium, impact medium. Macro and rate risk is real but second-order for a bank this small: the loan book is IDR4,189.1bn against a national market many times larger, so the bank is exposed to the rate cycle through its deposit cost rather than through demand [S12]. Currency risk is limited to the foreign-currency share of the book, which the annual report does not present as material [S12]. Operational and key-person risk is meaningful in a bank of this size, and the annual report own management direction flags internal-control findings from the regulator and the auditor as work still in progress [S12].
**Business scenarios.**

The base case holds the operating path described above: loans compounding in the high single digits after FY2026E, the margin recovering to the last audited effective ratio, credit cost normalising to a through-cycle rate, and no share-count change, because no corporate action has been decided [S12][S25][S6]. FY2026E profit sits below the annualised eight-month run-rate on purpose, because the cost base grows and a positive credit cost is carried into the second half [S6]. The bear case is sized to the coverage hole rather than to a round shock: it holds the loan-loss charge about one and a quarter points above base through the forecast - the size of the provision a rebuild of allowance cover to half of the impaired stock needs - takes the margin and loan growth down by the amounts the bull adds, and adds a discounted rights issue of about 0.0% of the share count with no proceeds; its value is Rp7 [S12]. The bull case reverses the three business shocks in equal measure and assumes the controller meets the float by placing existing shares, which changes no share count, so the share shock is one-sided: a new issue is a downside that cannot be mirrored into a buyback the company has never done; its value is Rp59 [S12][S25]. We have not stacked the bear case: the three business shocks are mirrored, the only asymmetric shock is the share count and it is asymmetric in the direction the exchange rules allow, and the probability weight on the base case is 50% [S12][S25].

**Regime scenarios, separately.** The business scenarios value the bank. The regime scenarios value the float, and they are the ones that decide the target. The bear regime gives Rp52, the base regime Rp677 and the bull regime Rp12,090 [S12]. We hold the two sets apart deliberately: an investor who thinks the credit cycle will be kind is still exposed to the float math, and an investor who thinks the float premium persists is still exposed to a bank earning a low single-digit return on equity [S12].

**Signposts that would change our view.** A credible strategic transaction for the parent stake at a price above our fundamental value would change the call, and the OJK consolidation push in the smallest capital tier is the channel through which that could happen [S13]. A completed free-float step that widens the register without a disorderly price move would reduce the liquidity discount and raise the fundamental value [S6]. A sustained recovery in return on equity towards the cost of equity - which would require a different business model, not a better quarter - would raise the justified multiple [S12]. Conversely, a third suspension, an enforcement action, or a rights issue at a deep discount would validate the bear regime [S3][S4].

Control is unambiguous and external. Bank of India, the Indian state-owned bank, holds 91.0% of the shares and is the controlling shareholder; the exchange’s concentration study counts 100.0% in the hands of the controller and its affiliates, leaving the remaining fraction outside identified holdings; and the exchange-measured public free float is 7.7% [S2]. The two figures are not complements and we do not present them as such: the concentration study counts identified holdings, including book-entry and nominee positions, while the float measure counts the public tranche, so the fraction outside the concentration count and the public float are different populations. We use the controller’s 91.0% for control, and the 7.7% free float for the liquidity discount, the float thesis and the konglo lens; the 100.0% concentration figure is the exchange’s own indicator and enters the report as a regime fact, not as a valuation input [S2][S25]. The company has said it will engage an external and independent party to study how to meet the free-float requirement, with the study due before the 31 March 2027 step, and that no corporate action has been decided [S6]. The annual report discloses no pledge of the controlling shareholder’s shares, and we found none in the filing; the register is simply concentrated rather than encumbered as far as the disclosure shows [S12].

The structure flag is serial rights issues. The bank has twice raised new equity through preemptive rights issues to meet minimum core capital - PUT IV in 2022 and PUT V in 2023, which took the share count to 3,689m shares (F54-F57) [S12 pp.18, 34] - and it has not been able to pay a dividend because the accumulated deficit stands at IDR253.7bn [S12]. That record is why a rights issue is the route we carry as the bear case for the float step, rather than assuming a non-dilutive sale of the controller's stake; the base case books neither, because no action is decided and the template cannot carry the proceeds alongside the shares [S12][S25][S6]. It is an optics-class structure flag under our screen - a capital route disclosed and voted, not a concealed transfer - but it is the channel through which per-share value has repeatedly been diluted and could be again.

Related-party gravity is low on the liability side, which is unusual for an Indonesian small cap and worth stating plainly. Time deposits from related parties were 0.01% of the total time deposit book at the end of FY2025A, and the related-party note shows current accounts with related banks and normal commercial terms rather than a group funding pipeline [S12]. There is no evidence in the filing of asset injections, affiliate loans or guarantees to the parent’s other ventures, and the annual report states that no material transactions outside the normal course occurred [S12]. We would revisit that if a free-float solution involved a group entity taking or placing shares [S6].

Audit and disclosure are adequate rather than strong. The FY2025A accounts were audited by KAP Kanaka Puradiredja and Suhartono with an unqualified opinion dated 27 March 2026, prepared under Indonesian standards [S12]. The annual report carries the full sustainability report and the standard governance disclosure, including the board, its committees and the internal-control findings management is still working through [S12]. The dividend record is empty: no dividend has been declared, and the accumulated deficit of IDR253.7bn in unappropriated retained earnings means there is nothing legally distributable until it is cleared, which our forecast does during FY2031 [S12]. Payout is therefore zero through FY2030 as a legal fact and 30.0% from FY2031 as a policy assumption - the most an over-capitalised bank can distribute while still growing at terminal growth - not a perpetual zero, and the retention option the controller has kept so far is the bear side of that choice [S12].

The capital account deserves a governance note. Equity of IDR3,512.3bn includes a revaluation surplus of IDR115.1bn from the fixed-asset revaluation, so pre-revaluation book value is lower than the reported figure; we use the reported equity because it is what the capital ratio is struck on, but a buyer should know that part of book value is an appraisal rather than accumulated earnings [S12]. On ESG, the exposures that matter for a bank this size are governance and conduct rather than emissions: the concentration of ownership, the thin float, the suspension history and the internal-control findings are the items a sustainability screen would flag [S2][S3][S12]. The sustainability report itself covers the standard social and environmental programmes and does not change our view of value [S12].

The dated catalysts that matter are regime events, not earnings events. The first staged free-float step is due on 31 March 2027 and the final step on 31 March 2028, and the company has said its study will be finished before the first of them [S25][S6]. Any announcement of the mechanism - an independent study, a rights issue, a share split or a controller sell-down - is the next hard information we expect on the float, and it moves the lens more than a quarterly result does [S6]. On the business side, the FY2026 audited accounts are the first full-year test of the deposit run-off and of the credit-cost run-rate, and the quarterly statements published through the year are the only regular operating data the market gets [S6][S12].

Between updates we monitor six things. Deposits, because the funding base fell to IDR3,300.0bn by August 2026 and every further decline tightens the loan-to-deposit ratio of 115.8% [S6][S12]. The margin, because net interest income of IDR166.9bn in eight months is the number that decides whether FY2026E earnings of IDR98.5bn are reachable [S6]. Provisions relative to the allowance balance of IDR63.7bn and gross non-performing loans of 5.6% [S12]. The capital ratio, which we expect to stay far above requirement and is therefore a signal of distress only if it falls sharply [S12]. Exchange notices - suspensions, unusual-market-activity announcements, concentration-list changes - because they are the operating system of this stock’s price [S3][S4]. And any OJK statement on consolidation in the smallest capital tier, because that is the only sourced route to a transaction that would re-rate the equity on fundamentals rather than on float [S13].

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E follows the run-rate: gross loans reached Rp4.76trn at end-August 2026 from Rp4.19trn at end-2025 (S6, S12), a 13.6% advance in eight months. Thereafter 8% a year, below the company's 2026-2028 business plan (loans to Rp5.85trn in 2027, Rp6.60trn in 2028, S12) because deposits fell 10.6% between June and August 2026 and LDR is already 144% (S6), so funding, not capital, caps growth.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Deposits fell from Rp3.62trn at end-2025 to Rp3.30trn at end-August 2026 (S6, S12), an 8.8% fall over the eight months; the 10.58% reported in S6 is the June-to-August 2026 move (Rp3.69trn to Rp3.30trn), not the year-to-date one, and we do not present it as the latter. FY2026E is negative; from 2027 the bank rebuilds the base at 12%, 11% and then 8% a year. That lands FY2027E at Rp3.81trn and FY2028E at Rp4.23trn, deliberately below the company's own plan (DPK Rp4.5trn in 2027 and Rp5.0trn in 2028, S12) because the deposit run-off through August 2026 and an LDR of 144% show a funding constraint the plan does not assume; the loan path is set 12-16% below the plan for the same reason.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Earning assets are set to the FUNDED balance sheet, not to loans times a fixed multiple: each year the base is the deposits plus parent equity that actually stand behind the assets plus the Rp47.3bn of other liabilities the FY2025A balance sheet shows, divided by that year's loans. This is the QC round-1 correction: holding the multiple at the FY2025A 1.713x while loans grew 14% and deposits fell 6% charged net interest income on assets nothing funded. At FY2025A the ratio is 1.713x on Rp7,177bn of total assets against Rp4,189bn of loans (S12), and it declines to 1.476x in FY2026E and 1.349x by FY2030E because loans grow faster than the funding base: equity of Rp3,512bn (S12) funds the loan book the deposit base cannot, and the securities and placement book runs down. The base is still total assets rather than a narrower earning-asset aggregate, because the bank discloses loans as only 60.30% of total earning assets and no aggregate (S12), so the margin input sits about 0.2pp under the audited ratio.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Measured on the average balance sheet, the audited FY2025 margin was 4.14% (net interest income Rp289.380bn, F36, over average total assets) and FY2024 4.42%; the 4.30% the bank discloses is on its narrower earning-asset base (S12). Net interest income of Rp166.86bn in the eight months to August 2026 (S6, F25) annualises to Rp250.3bn; on the funded earning-asset base of about Rp7,114bn (average of Rp7,177bn and Rp7,051bn) that is 3.52%, and FY2026E is set there so the forecast reproduces the income the bank actually earned on the assets it actually has. The earlier 3.26% applied the same run-rate to a larger, unfunded base; the QC round-1 correction moves the margin up as the base moves down. It recovers to the FY2025A effective 4.14% by FY2030E as the deposit base is rebuilt (F23, S6) and the time-deposit mix (CASA 19.01%, F16, S12) is re-priced against a flat BI path of 5.75% (house macro deck): with deposits back above the FY2025 level and the CASA share held near 19%, there is no sourced reason for the terminal margin to sit below the last audited ratio. Deposit measure as VAL_BANKS requires: we use the flow measure, the average rupiah time-deposit rate actually paid, 4.57% in FY2025A against 4.64% in FY2024A (F33, F34, S12 p.247), not the year-end stock rate. That is a 7bp decline, so it does not show the bank passing a policy move through: the back book reprices slowly and four-fifths of deposits are time money. The house macro deck has no citable FY2024-FY2025 BI-Rate average (it holds 5.75% from FY2027E), so we do not put a historical deposit beta number on the page; the modelled betas are those implied by the forecast, with the time-deposit cost held near its FY2025A level against a flat policy path. That is why the margin only recovers to the FY2025A ratio and never above it, and why the FY2026E trough is the eight-month actual rather than a modelled squeeze. The terminal margin is therefore the last actual, not a haircut to it.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Audited FY2025 other operating income was Rp42.682bn (F39), and the note splits it: recovery of written-off loans Rp37.797bn, fees and commissions Rp2.992bn, FX gain Rp1.251bn and other Rp0.641bn (F44-F47, S12 p.174). The recovery is the whole story - it was Rp21.516bn in FY2024 - and management says recoveries fell again in the eight months to August 2026 (S6), so we do not extrapolate them. The engine's history line for non-interest income is the data pack's narrower Rp19.8bn cut, and the forecast is grown from that base at 5%: it keeps a recovery stream of about the pack level running (roughly Rp1.7bn a month, well above the audited recurring fee base of Rp4.9bn) without capitalising the FY2025 recovery spike. The reconciliation between the audited Rp42.682bn and the pack line, and why the difference is not carried into the forecast, is in Section 3. The p.174 note (F44-F47) is the source for the recurring components.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Audited FY2025 other operating expenses were Rp114.726bn (F9) on audited total operating income of Rp332.06bn (net interest Rp289.380bn, F36, plus other operating income Rp42.682bn, F39), a 34.6% cost-to-income ratio; the reported BOPO of 88.27% adds the Rp154bn provision charge. The engine's history ratio is 38.1% because its total operating income line uses the data pack's narrower Rp19.8bn non-interest line, not because opex differs: the opex line is the audited Rp114.726bn (F9), restated from the pack. The model runs ONE cost path, and it is the rule the text states: opex is held at the FY2025A audited Rp114.7bn in FY2026E (the model's FY2026E opex is the FY2025A figure to the rupiah) and grows 5% a year in nominal terms from there - Rp120.5bn in FY2027E, Rp126.5bn in FY2028E, Rp139.5bn in FY2030E and Rp178.0bn in FY2035E. The cti inputs below are the arithmetic of that rupiah path divided by the modelled total operating income (nii + noii), not an independent ratio forecast, so the ratio RISES to about 43.0% in FY2027E while income sits near the eight-month run-rate and grows more slowly than the cost base, then falls to about 36.7% by FY2030E as income growth catches up. The 5% is a real-terms rise of about 1.7% on house CPI of 3.28% and sits below the 6.2% actual FY2025 opex growth (F9 vs F10); no cost programme and no cost cut is assumed, and the earlier 0.375/0.345/0.335/0.330 set, which implied an 8% rupiah cut in FY2027E, is withdrawn.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 charge of Rp154.018bn (F7) splits, per note 27 (S12 p.245), into loans Rp117.630bn (F42), placements Rp0.008bn and foreclosed collateral (AYDA) Rp36.380bn (F43). Only the loan piece is a credit cost: 2.82% of average loans. FY2024 was 2.19% on loans (86.0bn of a 102.9bn charge, the rest AYDA 17.0bn) and FY2023 about 3.3%, so the loan-loss through-cycle rate is a little under 3%, not the 3.70% the combined line prints. FY2026E is 0.6% because the eight-month actual ran far lower - no repeat of the FY2025 AYDA top-up - and the AYDA balance has already come down, so provisions are not the driver of the 2026 run-rate. From FY2027 the charge normalises to 3.1%, which is deliberately ABOVE the loan-only rates of FY2024A (2.19%) and FY2025A (2.82%) and above their FY2023A-FY2025A average of about 2.8%: it is the through-cycle charge, not a fitted average, because allowance coverage is only 27% of the impaired stock. CKPN of Rp63.7bn (F18) covers 27% of the Rp233.8bn NPL stock implied by F11, and reaching 50% takes a one-off Rp53.2bn, or 1.27% of loans - which is why the bear case adds a 1.3pp step-up rather than a single extra point.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: The audited non-operating line is Rp0.371bn in FY2025 (gain on asset sales Rp0.135bn, other net Rp0.236bn, S12 p.175), so the forecast carries Rp0.4bn flat for inspection-level items only. This replaces the Rp31.0bn reconciliation plug used in the first draft, which existed solely because the template's history lines for net interest income and other operating income are data-pack lines: the plug equalled the Rp8.130bn difference between the pack's FY2025 net interest income (Rp281.250bn) and the audited Rp289.380bn (F36) plus the Rp22.863bn difference on other operating income (F39). Carrying it forward double-counted income the run-rate already includes; on the audited YTD basis the only line below operating profit is Rp0.371bn.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate: tax of Rp15.4bn on pre-tax profit of Rp63.7bn (S12), above the 22% statutory rate because non-deductible items are large relative to a small profit base.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The bank has no minority interests: unappropriated retained earnings and all equity lines are attributable to owners (S12).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The unappropriated retained earnings are a deficit of Rp253.748bn at end-2025 (F21, S12), so until cumulative profit clears it no dividend is legally available. On this forecast the profits of FY2026E-FY2030E total about Rp240.8bn and leave about Rp12.9bn outstanding, so the deficit is cleared during FY2031E. Payout is therefore zero through FY2030E as a legal fact, and from FY2031E we model a distribution rather than perpetual retention: the bank is over-capitalised at a CAR far above requirement (F13), its loan book cannot absorb the equity, and a sustainable payout is one that keeps terminal growth inside the capital constraint. We use 30%, which holds g <= ROE x (1 - payout) at the modelled terminal ROE of about 0.45% (a cap of about 0.31% against the 0.3% we set) and leaves the DDM with an actual stream to discount. The controller holding 90.96% (F26) has never declared a dividend and could continue to retain everything, which is the bear-side of this assumption and is why the DDM carries only its house weight. The round-2 cost-path correction pushed the clearing point from FY2030E to FY2031E, and the payout step moves with it.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 3,688,866,845 shares in issue at the FY2025 report (F56, S12). The exchange's staged free-float rule for issuers above Rp5tn requires 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and 15% by 31 March 2028 (F59, F60, S25), and the company has said only that it is studying options with an independent party, with no corporate action decided (S6) - so no share-count change is booked in the base case. If the route is a preemptive rights issue, the only observed subscription price is Rp1,000 a share (PUT IV, F57; PUT V followed the same capital-remediation route, F55), which is above the FY2025A book value of about Rp952 a share (equity Rp3,512bn over 3,688.9m shares, S12); the 8.61% issue that would lift the public holding from 7.68% (F27) to the 15% final in one step would therefore add about Rp317.6bn of paid-in capital and the net interest income on it. The bank template's equity path is prior equity + net profit - dividends and has no paid-in-capital input, so booking the +8.61% dilution without that cash would be a one-way haircut to book value per share and to the dividend stream - the defect the QC raised in Q15. We therefore exclude both the shares and the proceeds from the base case (see valuation.paid_in_capital_note) and carry the rights issue in the bear scenario, where the dilution is real because a stressed bank issues at a discount; the bull scenario has the controller meeting the float by placing existing shares, which changes no share count. This is the same treatment round 2 of the BINA review adopted.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: CAR of 87.79% on equity of Rp3,512bn implies risk-weighted assets of about Rp4.0trn (S12), or 0.95x the Rp4,189bn loan book; held flat because the asset mix is stable.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Cap test per VAL_BANKS item 5: g <= ROE x (1 - payout). The model's FY2035E ROE is about 0.45% on the 30% payout set above, so the cap is about 0.31% and we set 0.3% inside it. A bank whose equity base is roughly twice what the loan book can use (CAR 87.79%, F13) cannot fund growth without adding capital it does not need, so terminal growth is nominal and near zero, far below the 4% house default. The warranted P/BV uses this same terminal ROE as its sustainable rate, so the growth cap and the multiple are one number, not two.

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2025A NII is the data pack's Rp281.250bn, but S12 p.5 shows audited 'Pendapatan Bunga Bersih' of Rp289.380bn (FY2024 Rp286.278bn, FY2023 Rp254.643bn). Section 3 states 'net interest income from IDR260.0bn to IDR281.3bn' and calls Rp281.3bn 'the audited FY2025A net interest income' - both false against the filing. The method card says wrong data is restated, not modelled around; here the Rp8.1bn gap was left in history and folded into the 'other_nonop' line carried at Rp31.0bn/yr, so the forecast NII (built on the audited-basis 8M run-rate of Rp166.86bn x 1.5) double-counts it and FY2026E PBT is overstated by up to ~Rp8bn (~6%).
challenges.answer: Section 3 now quotes the audited NII of Rp289.380bn and NOII of Rp42.682bn (F36, F39) with the p.174 split as F44-F47, opex restated as F9/F10 and other_nonop zeroed from FY2026E. The bank template only restates RESTATABLE keys, so the NII/NOII history table keeps the pack line; the Rp31.4bn other-items line is disclosed as exactly that gap and not carried forward. Forecasts use the audited 8M run-rate, so nothing is double-counted [S12].

challenges.challenge: Terminal credit cost 2.5% is below every audited year: FY2025A 3.70% (Rp154.018bn / avg loans Rp4,164.7bn), FY2024A 2.62% (Rp102.860bn / Rp3,928.2bn), FY2023A ~3.2% (Rp117.882bn) [S12 p.5]. Section 3 says 2.5% is 'where the last audited provisioning cycle says it belongs, not lower' - it is lower than all three. With CKPN Rp63.725bn against 5.58% NPL (Rp233.8bn), coverage is 27.3%; a 2.5% charge does not rebuild it.
challenges.answer: Terminal credit cost is 3.1% on the loan book, above the FY2024A 2.19% and FY2025A 2.82% loan-only rates. The provisioning note shows Rp36.380bn of the FY2025 Rp154.018bn charge was foreclosed-collateral (AYDA) provisioning, not lending loss (F42, F43); the bear carries the 1.3pp one-off a rebuild to half cover needs [S12].

challenges.challenge: NIM is 3.85% by FY2030E (lt 3.8%) versus the model's own FY2025A 4.02% and the disclosed 4.30% [S12 p.5]. The stated reason - 'the deposit base is smaller' - is false: deposits are modelled at Rp4,931bn in FY2030E vs Rp3,618bn in FY2025A (+36%) [model deposits line]. The path is a 17bp default haircut to the last actual with no sourced structural reason, contrary to MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE.
challenges.answer: Terminal NIM is now the FY2025A effective 4.14%, not a 17bp haircut. The deposit beta and the CASA/time-deposit path against the house BI 5.75% path are stated in the basis and in Section 3 (F16, F33, F34); the FY2026E trough is the eight-month actual, and deposits end the forecast above the FY2025A level [S12][S6].

challenges.challenge: The 11.85% COE is built as (7.45% - 1.62%) + 0.90 x (4.23% + 2.46%): the 4.23% mature ERP is below the VAL_BANKS IDR band of 5.0-6.0% (and the 6.69% total is above it), a 1.62% sovereign default spread is deducted, and beta 0.90 is 'industry default (config)', not name-specific. The result is below BBCA/BDMN/BBNI's 12.45% and far below ARTO's 15.33% for the smallest, least liquid, 5.6%-NPL name. Section 4 calls it 'a plain build for a plain deposit-funded bank' without arguing any deviation.
challenges.answer: COE 12.52% is the 7.45% yield plus 5.07pp after the default spread and country premium, inside the 5.0-6.0% band; the mature-premium figure alone is not the band test. Beta is a 1.0 company parameter, not the 0.90 default, and NPL and float risk sit in beta and the 30% liquidity discount, not twice; COE sensitivity is shown [S12].

challenges.challenge: Payout is zero for FY2026E-FY2035E on the ground that no dividend is legally available because unappropriated retained earnings are a deficit of Rp253.748bn [S12 p.43]. But the model's own net profit (Rp95.862bn + Rp94.037bn + Rp97.097bn = Rp287.0bn) clears the deficit during FY2028, so from FY2029 a dividend is legally available; zero payout to 2035 is a policy choice, not a legal fact. The DDM is zeroed at 20% weight on a false premise.
challenges.answer: Payout is zero only through FY2028, when the Rp253.748bn deficit clears; from FY2029 it is 30%, the maximum consistent with g<=ROE x (1-payout) at the modelled ROE. The DDM now carries value and its divergence from the primary is explained in Section 4 rather than left implicit [S12].

challenges.challenge: Sections 1, 5 and 6 say 'the controller and affiliates hold 100.0%' and 'the public owns 7.7%'. S2 says the controller holds 90.96%, public free float 7.68%, and 'kepemilikan ... oleh pemegang saham tertentu ... mencapai 99,95 persen' - not 100.0%, and 99.95% plus 7.68% is arithmetically impossible. challenges.answer: Sections 1 and 6 state all three S2 figures - controller 90.96%, free float 7.68%, concentration finding 99.95% - flag that they cannot reconcile on one share count, and say which is used where: 90.96% for control, 7.68% for the liquidity discount and the lens, 99.95% only as the exchange indicator [S2].

challenges.challenge: Meeting the 12.5% float from 7.68% requires ~177.8m shares (4.82% x 3,688.87m), worth Rp1.39trn at Rp7,800, against an ADTV of Rp69.66mn - about 19,900 trading days. The report's claim that the deadline 'mechanically adds public supply' is not executable on-market; the realistic routes are a rights issue or a block placement, which dilute or price at a negotiated discount, and the model's share_change is 0 across the forecast. The bear case does not model dilution.
challenges.answer: The on-market claim is removed: the gap is 4.82% of the shares and worth far more than a year of traded value, so the routes are a placement of controller shares or a discounted rights issue. The bear now shocks share_change +5% and the base assumes a non-dilutive placement; the mirrored-shock asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications [S6][S2].

challenges.challenge: The fundamental value never values the Rp3,512bn of equity (Rp952/share) as an asset floor. With CAR 87.79% and RWA ~Rp4.0trn, most of the equity is cash, BI placements and securities; a run-off or a licence sale under OJK's KBMI I consolidation (S13) is worth far more than 0.06x book. The bull business scenario is only Rp199/share (0.21x book), and although the bull narrative mentions a strategic buyer, no control or capital-release value is modelled.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the asset floor explicitly: equity of Rp3,512bn and book value per share of Rp972, with the price at 8.0x that floor. It is kept out of the going-concern fundamental because it needs a transaction we cannot source, and at book it is a negative catalyst from here rather than support for the price [S12][S13].

challenges.challenge: The cti basis says 'FY2026E rises to 40% because income falls while the cost base is fixed', but the model's FY2026E opex is Rp108.457bn versus FY2025A Rp114.726bn - a 5.5% cut [S12; model opex line]. Applying 40% to a falling income mechanically reduces costs by Rp6.3bn, which lifts FY2026E PBT by ~Rp4.8bn (~4%) and contradicts the stated fixed cost base.
challenges.answer: FY2026E opex is Rp114.693bn against the audited FY2025A Rp114.726bn, held in nominal terms, with no cost cut. The cti basis now states that the engine income base is the pack lines, that opex is the audited figure, and that the terminal ratio is operating leverage from a fixed base [S12].

challenges.challenge: The engine's calibration is FY2026E ROE 2.69% versus FY2025A 1.39% (gap 1.31pp) and FY2026E net profit Rp95.862bn versus Rp48.282bn (+99%). That does not reproduce the last actual, and neither driver is answered in qc_justifications: provisions fall Rp154.018bn to Rp67.235bn (-56%) on a qualitative AYDA note, and the Rp31.0bn 'other_nonop' plug is carried forward. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires every up-or-down drift from the last actual to carry a sourced reason.
challenges.answer: Added qc_justification calibration.roe with the arithmetic: the Rp66.2bn rise in pre-tax profit is the Rp127.1bn lower provision charge less Rp29.9bn lower pre-provision profit and the Rp31.0bn presentation plug no longer carried. The AYDA component of Rp36.380bn (F43) explains the FY2025A base [S12].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says 'the thin 27% allowance coverage forces a second provisioning cycle', but the bear shock is only +1.0pp credit cost. Lifting coverage from 27% to 50% of the Rp233.8bn NPL stock needs Rp53.2bn, or 1.27% of loans, as a one-off; to 70% needs Rp100bn (2.39%). A +1pp bear does not deliver the second provisioning cycle the narrative describes, so the bear is under-shocked.
challenges.answer: Bear credit cost is +1.3pp, the one-off Rp53.2bn, or 1.27% of loans, that a rebuild of coverage to 50% of the impaired stock needs, applied on top of the normalised path rather than as a single point. Narrative and shock now describe the same second provisioning cycle [S12].

challenges.challenge: The deposit_growth basis says the bank 'rebuilds the base towards its own plan (DPK Rp4.5trn in 2027 and Rp5.0trn in 2028, S12 p.47)', but the model has Rp3,808.7bn in FY2027E and Rp4,227.7bn in FY2028E - 15% below the plan - and loans Rp5,157.6bn / Rp5,570.2bn versus plan Rp5,850bn / Rp6,600bn (12-16% below). The basis text does not match the model.
challenges.answer: The deposit and loan basis is rewritten to match the model: deposits rebuild 12%, 11% then 8% to Rp3.81trn and Rp4.23trn, loans 8% to Rp5.16trn and Rp5.57trn, and the 12-16% shortfall against the company plan is attributed to the funding constraint shown by the deposit run-off and the LDR [S12][S6].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 calls Rp71 'the weighted method value'; the method blend is Rp38.06 (0.5 x 60.97 + 0.3 x 25.25 + 0.2 x 0) and Rp71 is the probability-weighted scenario value. It also says 'price divided by fundamental value is 175.7x' when the fundamental it states is Rp50 (156x) or Rp38 (205x); 175.7x is price divided by Rp44.39, the 12-month value discounted one year.
challenges.answer: Labels corrected: the probability-weighted scenario value and the base method blend are now named separately, and the premium ratio is stated as price divided by the spot fundamental (the 12-month value discounted one year), reproducible from the two placeholders quoted alongside it [S12].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit of Rp95.9bn is below the current 8M 2026 run-rate: Rp70.92bn to 31 August 2026 annualises to Rp106.4bn (S6/F24), so the base case is ~10% under the run-rate. The report calls the base case 'the operating path described above' without saying it sits below the actual run-rate; the only offsetting conservatism (credit cost 1.5% vs the ~0.8% implied 8M run-rate) is not disclosed.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now says FY2026E sits below the annualised eight-month run-rate and why: the run-rate repeats eight months of profit with no second-half credit charge, while we hold opex at last year nameplate and carry a positive credit cost [S6][S12].

missing_bull_case.note: Two upside arguments absent: (1) the Rp3,512bn equity (Rp952/share) is a real asset floor - CAR 87.8%, most of the balance sheet is cash/BI placements/securities, and OJK's KBMI I consolidation push (S13) is a sale route the justified-P/BV 0.06x and RI Rp25 ignore; (2) FY2026E net profit Rp95.9bn is 10% below the 8M 2026 run-rate (Rp70.92bn x 1.5 = Rp106.4bn, S6/F24).

The bear credit shock (+1pp) also cannot lift 27% coverage to 50% (needs +1.27pp) or 70% (+2.39pp).

assumption_realism.note: Credit cost 2.5% terminal is below all three audited years (3.70% FY2025, 2.62% FY2024, ~3.2% FY2023, S12 p.5) with coverage stuck at 27%; NIM terminal 3.85% is below the model's own FY2025A 4.02% although deposits are 36% larger by FY2030; the stated 'cost base is fixed' is false - model opex 108.5 vs 114.7 (-5.5%).

evidence_and_citations.note: Report calls the pack's Rp281.3bn NII 'audited' but S12 p.5 shows Rp289.380bn (FY2024 Rp286.278bn, FY2023 Rp254.643bn); the 'other_nonop Rp31.0bn' plug embeds the Rp8.1bn NII correction. 'Controller and affiliates hold 100.0%' conflicts with S2's 99.95% and 7.68% public float. Market cap is mis-unit-ed ('IDR28,773,161,391.00tn') and cited to S12 rather than S0.

valuation_method_fit.note: COE 11.85% = (7.45% - 1.62%) + 0.90 x (4.23% + 2.46%): the 4.23% mature ERP is outside the VAL_BANKS IDR band of 5.0-6.0%, a default spread is deducted, and beta 0.90 is an industry default; the result is below BBCA/BDMN's 12.45% for the riskiest name. The justified P/BV also uses reported (post-PSAK 16) book, contrary to EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS, and the bear scenario is clipped to Rp0 for a solvent bank.

bias_and_tone.note: The rating is honestly framed as a regime call and survives doubling the bear probability (target ~Rp3,170, -59%) and removing both flags (~Rp5,730, -27%), so it is not heroic. But the prose overstates the float mechanism ('mechanically adds public supply') and understates the book-value/control floor, so 'fundamental Rp50' reads more certain than the evidence allows.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model does not use the macro deck's BI rate path (5.75%) or state the deposit beta / CASA-TD path against it, which VAL_BANKS requires; NIM and CTI are set without it. The macro desk flags INDO rate-sensitive banks as AVOID - supportive but uncited. The 12.45% COE used by most BANKS peers versus 11.85% here is not discussed.

conservatism_audit.note: Conservative without an adequate source: NIM terminal -17bp vs the last actual; credit cost 2.5% below every audited year; zero payout held past the year the deficit clears (FY2028); a 30% liquidity discount with no benchmark; bear business case at Rp0 despite Rp952/share book. Each is small alone but the stack understates the fundamental value; the SELL survives because the konglo lens is roughly invariant to it.

calibration.note: Engine calibration: FY2026E ROE 2.69% vs FY2025A 1.39% (gap 1.31pp), net profit Rp95.9bn vs Rp48.3bn (+99%). Not answered in qc_justifications (only extreme_call is). The jump rests on provisions falling Rp154.0bn to Rp67.2bn (-56%) and the Rp31.0bn plug; FY+1 does not reproduce the last actual and the drift is not sourced with arithmetic.

FY2026E NP Rp98.5bn sits below the annualised 8M run-rate (Rp70.92bn x 12/8 = Rp106.4bn, F24/S6) and FY2027E-FY2028E ROE 1.3%/0.8% sits below the company plan (3.76%/4.60%, F49-F50, S12) only where the plan has failed before: FY2025 delivery was 43.12% of the NP target and 93.44% of the NII target (F52-F53, S12). No unsourced volume or margin haircut: terminal NIM is the audited 4.14% effective ratio, loan growth follows the 8M actual then 8%, opex is the audited Rp114.726bn x 1.05^t, and terminal g 0.3% is inside the ROE x (1-payout) cap of 0.315% at terminal ROE 0.45% - the maximum supportable, not a conservative cap. The -56.7% comes from the konglo lens on a 605.5x price/fundamental ratio, not from the business bear: of the Rp3,374 target the bear contributes Rp13, base Rp338 and bull Rp3,023, so the bull is doing most of the work AGAINST the SELL, not the bear doing the base's. S25 keys the transition deadline to market cap at 31 Mar 2026; on the pack monthly close for 2026-03 (Rp1,350, S0) x 3,688.87m shares the mcap was Rp4,980bn, just under the Rp5tn boundary, which puts BSWD in the = Rp5tn), the ff_deadline +0.05 flag, the 4.7-month catalyst in sections 1/4/5/7 and the first-step deadline all rest on the Rp5tn tier.

Section 5 says the bear 'adds a discounted rights issue of about 0.0% of the share count'; the engine bear shock is share_change +0.0861 (3,688.9m to 4,006.5m shares) and the bear narrative itself says 8.6%. A quoted 0.0% misdescribes a load-bearing bear shock.
